To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Bayesian bivariate probit approach provides a statistically efficient and computationally feasible way to measure surgeon quality, (2) the model accounts for the correlation between morbidity and mortality and for the dependence of both outcomes on the characteristics of patients prior to treatment, (3) surgeon-specific quality indices can be used to evaluate surgeon quality relative to both absolute standards for morbility and mortality rates and relative to other surgeons within a department.
(1) surgeons who perform more complex surgeries are more likely to have a higher rate of complications and (2) surgeons who perform a greater number of surgeries have a lower rate of complications.

(i) the new information technologies at the hospital provide administrators and policymakers at the hospital with a great deal of information on both the characteristics and the outcomes associated with the patients of individual surgeons, and (ii) the Bayesian hierarchical bivariate model we have developed for estimating surgeon quality provides a statistically valid and efficient method for analyzing the data and for evaluating the performance of individual surgeons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a Bayesian hierarchical model for profiling surgeon performance.
the use of new information technology systems in hospitals and medical centers to measure and monitor surgeon performance.
developing a methodology for monitoring the quality of care provided by individual surgeons.
